entry: Set of strings whose symbols are drawn from a fixed alphabet, studied in logic, mathematics, computer science and linguistics. The symbols concatenate into strings called words, and words that belong to a language are its well-formed words. Languages are often defined by a [[Grammar|formal grammar]], such as a regular or context-free grammar. In computer science, they underpin the grammars of [[Programming language|programming languages]] and controlled natural languages. In computational complexity theory, decision problems are typically defined as formal languages. In logic and the foundations of mathematics, they represent the syntax of axiomatic systems. Formal language theory grew out of linguistics. In the mid-19th century, [[George Boole]] established [[Boolean algebra]], and [[Gottlob Frege]] later attempted to realize Leibniz's ideas through a notation first outlined in *Begriffsschrift* (1879). [[Noam Chomsky]] devised the Chomsky hierarchy, an abstract classification of formal and natural languages.

Pungent colorless gas and the simplest [[Aldehyde|aldehyde]] (CH₂O), systematically named methanal. It is used mainly to make industrial [[Resin|resins]] for particleboard, coatings, plastics, paper and textiles. A solution of about 5% in water serves as a disinfectant and fumigant, and a solution of about 37% preserves tissue samples. Global production was estimated at 26 million tons per year in 2024. Commercial formalin is usually stabilized with a small amount of [[Methanol|methanol]] to suppress oxidation and polymerization. Formaldehyde also occurs naturally, derived from the degradation of serine, dimethylglycine and [[Lipid|lipids]]. It is classified as a Group 1 [[Carcinogen|carcinogen]] and can cause respiratory and skin irritation on exposure.

headword: Formation and evolution of the Solar System
sort_key: formation and evolution of the solar system
entry: Process by which the Solar System formed from a collapsing [[Molecular cloud|molecular cloud]] about 4.6 billion years ago and evolved into its present form. Most of the collapsing mass gathered at the center to form the Sun, while the rest flattened into a protoplanetary disk from which the planets, moons, asteroids and other small bodies formed. The standard model, the [[Nebular hypothesis|nebular hypothesis]], was developed in the 18th century by Emanuel Swedenborg, [[Immanuel Kant]] and [[Pierre-Simon Laplace]]. Its chief objection, that it could not explain the Sun's relative lack of angular momentum, was set aside after studies from the early 1980s showed young stars surrounded by discs of dust and gas. Later evolution included giant collisions, possibly producing Earth's Moon, and planetary migration, which shaped the present structure. In roughly five billion years the Sun will become a [[Red giant|red giant]], shed its outer layers as a [[Planetary nebula|planetary nebula]] and leave a [[White dwarf|white dwarf]].

Simplest [[Carboxylic acid|carboxylic acid]] (HCOOH), named from the Latin *formica*, meaning ant. It occurs naturally in some [[Ant|ants]] and is an important intermediate in chemical synthesis. In 1671, English naturalist John Ray first described isolating it by distilling large numbers of ants. Industrially it is produced from [[Carbon monoxide|carbon monoxide]], a process Marcellin Berthelot developed in 1855. Formic acid is about ten times stronger than [[Acetic acid|acetic acid]], with a pKa of 3.745 against 4.756. Since the late 1960s, byproduct supplies from acetic acid production have made it available in quantity, and it is now used as a preservative and antibacterial in [[Livestock|livestock]] feed.

Concise symbolic way of expressing information, as in a mathematical or [[Chemical formula|chemical formula]]. In mathematics, a formula is an [[Equation|equation]] or inequality relating one expression to another, and the most important formulas are theorems. Mathematicians write quantities as single letters, so the volume of a sphere of radius r is V = 4/3πr³. An expression such as 8x − 5 denotes an object, while a formula such as 8x − 5 ≥ 3 states a fact about it. In [[Mathematical logic|mathematical logic]], a formula is an entity built from the symbols and formation rules of a logical language. In chemistry, a formula gives the proportions of atoms in a compound: H₂O is water, with two hydrogen atoms for each oxygen atom. Newton's second law is expressed as F = ma.

Highest class of international open-wheel [[Auto racing|auto racing]], sanctioned by the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA). The word formula refers to the set of rules all cars must follow. The World Championship began in 1950 with the British Grand Prix at Silverstone Circuit, and each season consists of Grands Prix held on purpose-built circuits and closed roads. Points decide two annual championships, for drivers and for constructors, now synonymous with teams. [[Juan Manuel Fangio]] won five drivers' titles, a record that stood for 46 years until [[Michael Schumacher]] won his sixth in 2003. Cars rely on aerodynamic downforce for the highest cornering speeds of any regulated road-course racing car. The cost cap for the 2026 season is US$215 million, and six of the eleven teams are based in the United Kingdom.

1994 American comedy-drama film directed by [[Robert Zemeckis]]. Adapted from Winston Groom's 1986 novel, it stars [[Tom Hanks]] as an Alabama man whose life spans key episodes of 20th-century U.S. history. Released by [[Paramount Pictures]] on July 6, 1994, it earned over US$678 million worldwide on a $55 million budget and was the second-highest-grossing film of 1994, behind *The Lion King*. It won six [[Academy Awards|Academy Awards]], including Best Picture and Best Director, and in 2011 the [[Library of Congress|Library of Congress]] selected it for the National Film Registry.

Coastal city in [[Florida]], 30 miles (48 km) north of [[Miami]] on the Atlantic Ocean. It is the seat of Broward County and its most populous city, with 182,760 residents at the 2020 census. Named after a series of forts built by the United States during the Second Seminole War, it was built in 1838 and first incorporated in 1911. Nicknamed the Venice of America for its 165 miles of inland waterways, it has a diversified economy in marine industries, finance, aerospace and film, as well as [[Tourism|tourism]]. Nearly four million cruise passengers pass through Port Everglades each year, making it the world's third-busiest cruise port.

City in [[Texas]], county seat of Tarrant County and second-largest city in the [[Dallas–Fort Worth metroplex|Dallas–Fort Worth metroplex]]. Established in 1849 as an army outpost on the Trinity River, it was long a center of the Texas Longhorn cattle trade and retains its Western heritage. Its population was estimated at 1,028,117 in 2025, making it the 10th-most populous U.S. city. The Kimbell Art Museum was designed by [[Louis Kahn|Louis Kahn]], and the Amon Carter Museum of American Art by [[Philip Johnson|Philip Johnson]]. The city hosts the Van Cliburn International Piano Competition. Several multinational companies, including Bell Textron and [[American Airlines|American Airlines]], are headquartered there.

State capital and largest city of Ceará, on the northeastern coast of Brazil (pop., 2025: 2,578,483). It is Brazil's fourth-most-populous city and forms the core of a [[Metropolitan area|metropolitan area]] of almost 4 million people. Its name means fortress in Portuguese. Portuguese settlement began in 1603 around a fort, the settlement was officially founded as a village in 1726, and it became state capital in 1799. Fortaleza is an industrial and commercial center and, according to Brazil's Ministry of Tourism, the country's fourth-most visited destination. The BR-116, the country's most important highway, starts there. The city has a [[Tropical climate|tropical wet and dry climate]] with high temperatures and humidity, moderated by ocean winds. It is 5,608 kilometres (3,485 mi) from [[Lisbon|Lisbon]], Portugal, and one of the three leading cities of the Northeast with [[Recife|Recife]].

2017 free-to-play online video game and platform developed by Epic Games, in which several game modes share one engine. Its Battle Royale mode, in which up to 100 players fight to be the last one standing, became a cultural phenomenon, drawing more than 125 million players in less than a year. The cooperative Save the World mode pits up to four players against [[Zombie|zombie-like creatures]] while they build defenses. Fortnite as a whole generated $9 billion in gross revenue up to December 2019, one of the highest-grossing media franchises of all time. Most game modes support cross-platform play across consoles, PCs and mobile devices.

Third-generation, compiled, imperative [[Programming language|programming language]] designed for numeric computation and scientific computing. Developed by [[IBM|IBM]] under a team led by John Backus, with a reference manual released in 1956, it is widely used for numerical weather prediction, computational fluid dynamics, plasma physics and crystallography. It remains a popular language for high-performance computing, and programs that benchmark the world's fastest [[Supercomputer|supercomputers]] are written in it. A 1966 ANSI standard limited the proliferation of compilers with slightly different syntax. Later standards added structured programming (Fortran 77), modular programming (Fortran 90), parallel computing (Fortran 95) and [[Object-oriented programming|object-oriented programming]] (Fortran 2003).

Slender, cat-like [[Mammal|mammal]] (*Cryptoprocta ferox*) endemic to [[Madagascar|Madagascar]], the largest mammalian carnivore on the island. It has been compared to a small [[Cougar|cougar]], and adults weigh between 5.5 and 8.6 kg. [[Lemur|Lemurs]] make up more than half its diet, and litters range from one to six pups. Life expectancy in captivity is about 20 years. The fossa is listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, and Malagasy taboo, or fady, often protects it, but habitat destruction is its greatest threat. Genetic studies place it in the family Eupleridae, and carnivorans are now thought to have colonized Madagascar once, around 18–20 million years ago.

Preserved remains, impression or trace of a once-living thing from a past geological age. Examples include bones, shells, exoskeletons, objects preserved in [[Amber|amber]], petrified wood and DNA remnants. The totality of fossils is the fossil record, which is incomplete but sufficient to show the broad pattern of life's diversification on Earth. Body fossils preserve parts of an organism, usually mineralized tissues such as bones and teeth, while trace fossils record activity such as tracks or [[Feces|feces]]. The oldest fossils are around 3.48 to 4.1 billion years old. Radiometric dating, developed in the early 20th century, allowed the absolute ages of fossils to be measured. The largest known is a *Sequoia* sp. measuring 88 m (289 ft) at Coaldale, Nevada. Ancient peoples also collected fossils: Paleolithic stone knives had fossil echinoderms set at the grip, and Egyptian temples kept fossil bones of hippo-like species.

Pendulum named after French physicist [[Léon Foucault|Léon Foucault]], conceived to demonstrate Earth's rotation. As the Earth turns, the plane of a long, heavy pendulum's swing appears to change, an effect greatest at the poles and absent at the [[Equator|equator]]. Foucault first exhibited one in February 1851 at the [[Paris|Paris]] Observatory, then hung a 28-kilogram bob from a 67-metre wire under the dome of the Panthéon. There the plane of swing turned clockwise about 11.3° per hour, completing a full circle in about 31.8 hours. Foucault demonstrated the same rotation with a gyroscope in 1852.

Element of a structure that connects it to the ground, or more rarely to water, transferring its loads to the soil or rock. Foundations are generally classed as shallow or deep, and foundation engineering applies soil and rock mechanics to their design. Foundations spread weight over a large area to avoid overloading the [[Soil|soil]] and causing unequal settlement, anchor structures against [[Earthquake|earthquakes]], [[Flood|floods]], droughts, frost heaves and wind, and provide a level surface for construction. Shallow foundations, often called footings, are typically about a meter deep; the spread footing is a common type, a strip or pad of [[Concrete|concrete]] that transfers weight from walls and columns to the soil or bedrock. Rubble-trench foundations are shallow trenches filled with stone that extend below the frost line. Historically, buildings rested on padstones or dry stone, and timber pilings were used on soft or wet ground.

Readymade sculpture, a porcelain urinal signed "R. Mutt", attributed to [[Marcel Duchamp|Marcel Duchamp]] and first shown in 1917. Duchamp regarded readymades as everyday objects raised to the dignity of art by the artist's choice. He submitted it in April 1917 to the inaugural exhibition of the Society of Independent Artists in [[New York City|New York]]. Its rules accepted all works from paying artists, but the board kept the work hidden during the show, and Duchamp resigned in protest. The original is lost. Alfred Stieglitz photographed it for the [[Dada|Dada]] journal *The Blind Man*, and sixteen replicas were made to Duchamp's approval in the 1950s and 1960s. Art historians regard it as a landmark of 20th-century [[Avant-garde|avant-garde]] art. Glyn Thompson has identified the handwriting on the urinal as that of Elsa von Freytag-Loringhoven, and some have proposed that she made the original.

Four riders in the [[Book of Revelation|Book of Revelation]] of the New Testament, often identified as Conquest, War, Famine and Death. The Lamb opens the first four of seven seals, and the riders go out on white, red, black and pale horses. The first carries a bow and a crown, the second a sword, the third a pair of scales, and the fourth, Death, is accompanied by [[Hades|Hades]]. They are given authority over a quarter of the Earth to kill with sword, famine and plague. The text is attributed to John of Patmos and dated to about AD 95. [[Christianity|Christianity]] typically interprets the riders as harbingers of the Last Judgment.

Core framework of [[Buddhism|Buddhist]] doctrine, traditionally identified as the Buddha's first teaching. The four truths are dukkha, suffering or unsatisfactoriness, the inherent instability of transient existence; samudaya, its origin in craving and attachment; nirodha, its cessation through letting go of craving, which is called [[Nirvana|nirvana]]; and marga, the path to that release, the Noble Eightfold Path. Scholars have debated since the 19th century whether the formulation was a later development. Carol S. Anderson proposes that the truths became central to the Theravāda tradition by about the 5th century CE. The Mahāyāna tradition gives them less prominence.

Mathematical extension of three-dimensional [[Euclidean space|Euclidean space]] in which each point requires four coordinates, such as (x, y, z, w). Its regular polytopes include the [[Tesseract|tesseract]], the four-dimensional analogue of the cube. Ludwig Schläfli described Euclidean spaces of any dimension in 1852 and found six regular polytopes in four dimensions, though his work was published only in 1901. [[William Rowan Hamilton|William Rowan Hamilton]] defined the quaternions in 1843. In 1908 Hermann Minkowski introduced a four-dimensional spacetime combining three spatial dimensions with time, the framework of special relativity.

Type of [[Internal combustion engine|internal combustion engine]] in which the piston completes four strokes while turning the crankshaft. The strokes are intake, which draws in an air-fuel mixture; compression; combustion, or power, in which ignition drives the piston back down to produce work; and exhaust, which expels the spent gases. Ignition comes from a spark plug in gasoline engines and from heat generated by high compression in [[Diesel engine|diesel engines]]. German engineer [[Nicolaus Otto|Nikolaus August Otto]] demonstrated a practical four-stroke engine in 1876. The design is the most common for motorized land transport, used in automobiles, [[Truck|trucks]], diesel trains, light aircraft and motorcycles. Its main alternative is the two-stroke cycle.

Branch of mathematics that studies how general functions can be represented or approximated by sums of trigonometric functions or complex exponentials. It is named after [[Joseph Fourier|Joseph Fourier]], who showed that such representations greatly simplify the study of heat transfer, and it grew out of the study of [[Fourier series|Fourier series]]. Decomposing a function into oscillatory components is called Fourier analysis, and rebuilding it is Fourier synthesis. Applied to a sampled signal, it gives the amplitudes of sines and cosines at frequencies that are multiples of 1/T, a basis of [[Signal processing|signal processing]]. The field has been extended to [[Harmonic analysis|harmonic analysis]] on general groups and applies in [[Acoustics|acoustics]], optics, probability and number theory.

Expansion of a periodic function as an infinite sum of sine and cosine terms. [[Joseph Fourier|Joseph Fourier]] used such series to solve the [[Heat equation|heat equation]], arguing in an 1807 memoir on heat propagation that arbitrary functions could be expressed this way. The method makes many problems easier because the derivatives of trigonometric functions follow simple patterns. Fourier series cannot approximate arbitrary functions, since many have series that do not converge, but smooth, well-behaved functions converge to the original. Their coefficients are integrals of the function multiplied by sines and cosines over one period. The series are closely related to the [[Fourier transform|Fourier transform]], which handles functions that are not periodic, and they are used in [[Electrical engineering|electrical engineering]] and [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]].

Integral transform that converts a function of time or space into a function describing the frequencies present in it. The output is a complex-valued function of frequency, analogous to decomposing the sound of a musical chord into the intensities of its pitches. Functions localized in time have transforms spread across frequency, and vice versa, a relationship known as the uncertainty principle. The [[Gaussian function|Gaussian function]] is the critical case, and its Fourier transform is another Gaussian. [[Joseph Fourier|Joseph Fourier]] introduced sine and cosine transforms in his study of heat transfer, where Gaussians appear as solutions of the [[Heat equation|heat equation]]. The transform generalizes to functions of several variables and is central to the study of waves and [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]]. The [[Fast Fourier transform|fast Fourier transform]] is an algorithm for computing the discrete Fourier transform.

American commercial broadcast television network, launched by News Corporation on October 9, 1986, as a competitor to ABC, [[CBS|CBS]] and [[NBC|NBC]]. It was the most-watched American network in total viewership in the 2007–08 season and the highest-rated free-to-air network among viewers aged 18–49 from 2004 to 2012 and from 2020 to 2021. Fox has no news division and relies on [[Fox News|Fox News]] and related 24-hour channels for news. Its programming has included [[The Simpsons|The Simpsons]] and [[Family Guy|Family Guy]], and it has broadcast [[National Football League|National Football League]] games. Its headquarters are in [[New York City|New York City]].
